vly.ai has just been acquired by Freebuff! 🎉 I started vly two years ago while still in college. Since then, I’ve dropped out, went to the ER over 3 times, and pulled 100+ all-nighters to bring my vision of free coding agents to life. Now, we’re proud to announce that Freebuff has acquired vly’s underlying technology to make sure you never have to pay for AI ever again. Thank you to James Grugett and our incredible team for the best outcome I could have asked for. ❤️ Freebuff is building 100% free versions of every AI tool out there — starting with coding agents. We specialize in batch-spend for cost-optimized models and highly-targeted advertisements & data environments. We just made Lovable / Replit / Base44 100% free with vly. We also made free versions of Claude Code, Codex, ChatGPT, and more. Soon, you’ll see free versions of every piece of AI tool out there that wouldn’t even accept payments even if you tried. Freebuff is building the future of software platforms in the age of AI. vly is just the beginning.

Just won Most Technical Hack at University of California, Berkeley 's AI Hackathon! We built a tool that has the potential to accelerate cancer drug discovery: a multi-agent system that takes a tumor mutation profile and tells you which drugs might actually work, and why. -> Workbench: upload a LUAD mutation CSV, and a knowledge graph + LLM pipeline maps your mutations onto activated pathways, identifies coverage gaps, and routes to targeted therapies. Where the graph has no direct answer (which happens more than you'd think), an ML classifier trained on DepMap LUAD data predicts pathway vulnerabilities. It flags the gap, makes a call, and labels it as ML-predicted, so a clinician or researcher knows exactly what to trust. The system doesn't just return drugs. It generates a mechanistic report citing the exact subgraph it traversed, since clinical AI that can’t show its work isn’t useful to researchers in the field. It was invaluable to get real-time 1:1 technical feedback from Fetch.ai , Redis , and Annapurna Labs , and the chance to demo to Anthropic 's team in person. Huge thanks to my amazing teammates Charity G. , Shruti Shah , and Shivnarain Sarin for shipping something real under serious time pressure, and thanks to the Cal Hacks team for the well-run event!

I'm excited to announce that the team at Adam Biotech and I are heading to Founders, Inc. for their Offseason program in SF this summer. We'll be surrounded by some of the world's brightest engineers and founders for six weeks as we finish our product and get it into labs. When we found out that we were accepted to Founders, Inc., our faces hurt from all the smiling. But now it's time to lock in harder than ever before. Accurate bioprinting means better preclinical validation models, meaning drug researchers can focus their energy on the drugs that will actually succeed in human trials. Millions of Americans with cancer, Alzheimer's, and so many other awful diseases are waiting for their treatments, and the pipeline to get those treatments starts with a bioprinter that doesn't fail. Huge thanks to Dharshini Maru , Abraham Hengyucius , and Jamison Schmidt for being one of the most passionate and hungry teams out there. Building the first comprehensive failure detection model for bioprinting is a hard problem to solve, and I can't think of a better team to do it with. If anyone is working in biotech or tissue engineering in SF this summer, please reach out! Would love to connect.

Did you know Bioengineers Without Borders at UW once traveled all the way to Uganda? This past Friday, our club hosted BWB History Night. It was an enlightening evening dedicated to celebrating the milestones, past projects, and accomplishments that have defined the club since 2014. We also took a look at the exciting work and progress of our current sub-teams. Founded on a mission to develop low-cost, accessible, and sustainable medical technologies, it's inspiring to see how much BWB has accomplished over the years. More than that, reflecting on that history has only deepened our focus on what's ahead. We look forward to more events, more workshops, and continued progress toward a more sustainable future for medical devices. Interested in being part of the next chapter? Stay tuned for our annual Fall Launch in October, and keep up with us here and on Instagram @uw_bwb!

16 years ago, a member of the Afghan Police helped a member of the Taliban enter our base disguised as a "detainee," then released him from his cell with access to an RPG & small arms, with the intent of letting him shoot down an Osprey. He aimed the RPG on an Osprey taking off only 100 meters away: an easy kill on the Osprey and its passengers, Navy SEAL Vice Admiral Robert Hardward & his staff. They would all easily have been killed if not for a quick thinking Ken McGonigle who saw him aiming and opened fire on him, causing him to retreat and abandon his attempt. His retreat was into our own jail, forcing us to attack a fortified structure on our own base. Ken McGonigle, Pfc Gammone and Lance Corporal Cornelius all charged into the fight to take out the threat and became Fallen Heroes. I will never forget them and hope you can keep them and their families in your thoughts and prayers.

What happens when you just start asking for what you want? (YC startups, free food) I found out in 2 completely different scenarios: 1. Sent 50+ cold DMs to YC founders without a job posting and pitched myself for a growth and marketing with them. A few replied. One ended in a job offer with OpenTrade (YC s26) . The postings might not be there, but I’ve come to learn that startups are ALWAYS hiring the right people. 2. On my flight back from Istanbul, I was still hungry after the first meal. I hesitated to ask for more food. Why? Because no one ever does it. But why not me? So I asked if they have leftovers in the back. And I got an extra meal for free. (shoutout Onur) The opportunities you want might not be advertised on LinkedIn or Indeed. But it never hurts to ask. p.s. if you’re a Wordle champ and play the LinkedIn minigames daily, check out OpenTrade (YC s26) for fun investing minigames and let me know what you think

In many ways, the work of a student is easy. We risk very little, yet enjoy a position over those who offer up their knowledge and their selves to our judgment. We enter the classroom carelessly, expecting our professors to serve us the fruits of their lifelong labor. But the bitter truth we students must face is that, in the grand scheme of things, these titans of the corporate world are sacrificing their most precious gift for us: their time. Having weathered the trials of extraordinary careers, rather than devoting well-deserved rest to family, loved ones, and personal pursuits, they choose to stand before us to illuminate our minds. Minds that, all too often, fail to grasp the sheer depth and beauty of the canvas being painted right before our eyes. In my final quarter, I experienced something extraordinary: a revelation that rocked me to my core, evoking that quiet reverence that stills the chest before the "Mona Lisa" or beneath the vaults of the "Sistine Chapel". That experience was the MGMT 550: CEO And Board Governance class at the Foster School of Business, taught by true virtuosos of their craft: Jeff R. (President and CEO at Premera Blue Cross) and Connie R. Collingsworth (Former COO Gates Foundation). This class gave me something infinitely greater than knowledge. It gave me faith and the conviction that one day I too, will bring meaningful value to society and the world, following the example of our distinguished guest lecturers: Jim Donald, Sunny Gupta , Brad Tilden, Amy Humphreys , Annie Young-Scrivner Jim Lico , Preston Feight, and many others. If my voice carried the strength of a clarion call, I would urge everyone who refuses the status quo, everyone who longs not only to know this world but to open themselves up to it in return, to take this class. For like Santiago in "The Alchemist", I spent years wandering the world in search of treasure, only to realize that the purest gold had been right where it all began all along, at the University of Washington. P.S. This monologue is my quiet homage to Brad Bird and his "Ratatouille", which offered the world a poignant reminder of how easy it is to judge the work of others, and how truly noble are those who risk creating and giving.

I spent years believing I was just "adaptable." The truth? I was just good at reading rooms and editing myself down to whatever version made other people comfortable. It started early, but the habit really took root through the Naval Academy and into my corporate career. I built a successful life out of fitting in seamlessly. The problem with building a life around what the room wants is that eventually, there’s no room left for you. Lately, I’m focused on a different skill: showing up without the edit. A few weeks ago I wrapped up my first tour in government, first as an advisor for R&D policy in the White House Office of Pandemic Preparedness and Response Policy (Jul 2024-Jan 2025), and then as a Biosecurity Fellow at DARPA's Biological Technologies Office (2025-2026). Working with exceptional colleagues to help protect the United States from biological threats, both natural, accidental, and deliberate, was an extraordinary privilege that I am very grateful for. While I am proud of what we accomplished, working in government during this time was full of challenges, including the difficulty of interagency coordination and policymaking, the increasing complexity of defending against future biological threats, and an extraordinarily polarized, click-chasing media and political environment that degrades Americans' trust in government, in science, and in each other. Trust, it seems to me, is the special sauce that makes any complex social system, including government, work. But it isn't cheap, nor should it be. Towards the end of my time at DARPA, I had the chance to spend time thinking about how to build trusted and trustworthy systems to prevent a malicious actor (whether a terrorist or a rogue state) from using increasingly capable AI tools to build and deploy biological weapons, while also making sure that the vast majority of legitimate scientists can still use AI to unlock beneficial advances we haven't even dreamed of yet. This, it turns out, is a hard problem-but a motivating one! As I take my next professional step, I'm excited to keep working on this challenge at RAND's Center for AI, Security, and Technology, where I'm now an AI & Biosecurity Research Resident.

This past week, I had the pleasure of volunteering with Verdafield: Science in the Park during their rocketry‑themed program. As someone passionate about engineering outreach, I’m a big believer that college students should actively seek opportunities to mentor the next generation and develop their own leadership skills in the process. For my first time working with kids and rockets, I went in thinking my limited rocketry knowledge would be the bottleneck. Turns out, the real challenges came from the kids. A few takeaways from the week: • Meet kids where they are They don’t need a propulsion lecture; they need someone patient enough to show them how to cut a straight line and cheer when they get it right. For instance, some kids didn’t have prior experience with box cutters or even scissors, which we solved by having a safety demonstration and then correcting them based off that. • Instructions matter more than you think Our parachute-crafting activity had a lot of “creative freedoms” which is code for “chaos.” Kids thrive when the steps are clear and the diagrams look like the final product. • Elementary schools have recess for a reason Long lectures aren’t fun for kids and our first day was lecture-heavy which we realized halfway through. We ended up having lunch early that day, and for subsequent days, we had breaks every 60-80 minutes which worked out nicely. • Group work is rocket fuel Once we realized most kids couldn’t build a rocket solo, we switched to teams. My ROTC brain immediately went, “Ah yes, a Group Leadership Project,” and then started writing org charts based on which kids work well together. We also minimized interpersonal friction points by using OpenRocket to make the best rocket as opposed to opinions. On an amusing note, ROTC unintentionally makes great teachers. All that focus on people, structure, and mentorship translates surprisingly well to camp instruction. The culmination of that group work was a rocket that hit 500+ feet at 60 Acres (I let the kids record that video so pardon the language). There was also a bottle rocket with 67 fins. Yeah, six-seven. Can’t beat the magical numbers. Huge thanks to camp instructors Thomas Coffee and Shuonan Dong for letting me volunteer. I’m excited for next week’s bigger class which will be a doozy.
